Course: Calculus I for Biological and Social Sciences. Section: 0. Course Overview. Content: \addcontentslinetocsection0. Course Overview The source textbook covers twelve chapters that blend standard single- and multivariable calculus with discrete-time modeling, differential equations, linear algebra, and probability/statistics --- the toolkit most commonly used in biology and social-science quantitative courses. Twelve chapters is more material than a single semester of ``Calculus 1'' typically covers, so this breakdown makes the following working assumption, stated here explicitly: \small Assumption. The textbook is delivered across a two-semester sequence. Calculus I (this course) corresponds to Chapters 1--6 (precalculus review through integration). Calculus II corresponds to Chapters 7--12 (integration techniques through probability and statistics) and is included here so the breakdown reflects the complete table of contents and shows how Calculus I feeds into it. If your program instead runs this material as a single accelerated semester, a three-quarter sequence, or omits later chapters, the six modules below can be regrouped or trimmed without changing their internal structure. \paragraphAudience and emphasis Students are primarily biology, ecology, pre-health, and social-science majors. Motivating examples throughout the course are drawn from population growth, drug kinetics, epidemiology, ecological interactions, demography, and data analysis rather than physics. \paragraphAsterisk convention Following the textbook's own convention, topics marked with an asterisk (*) are optional or enrichment material -- deeper rigor (e.g.\ formal \varepsilon--\delta limits), extensions of core ideas (e.g.\ stability of recurrence equations), or additional modeling examples. input_text: Course: Calculus I for Biological and Social Sciences. Section: 1. Overall Prerequisites (Before Calculus I). Content: \addcontentslinetocsection1. Overall Prerequisites (Before Calculus I) Algebra: manipulating and solving linear, polynomial, and rational equations and inequalities; working with exponents and radicals. Functions and graphs: function notation, domain and range, composition, and basic graph reading. Geometry: equations of lines and circles; basic coordinate geometry. Trigonometry: the unit circle, radian measure, and core identities. Exponentials and logarithms: laws of exponents and logarithms, and the relationship between them. Complex numbers: arithmetic of complex numbers and the quadratic formula for non-real roots. Chapter 1 of the course is itself a diagnostic-and-review chapter, so gaps in the list above are expected to be identified and remediated in the first two weeks rather than assumed away.

Content: \MajorTopics Formal definition of the derivative Properties of the derivative: interpretation; differentiability vs.\ continuity The power rule and derivatives of polynomials The product and quotient rules; derivatives of rational and power functions The chain rule (with proof) Implicit functions, implicit differentiation, and related rates Higher derivatives Derivatives of trigonometric, exponential, inverse, and logarithmic functions; the inverse tangent function Linear approximation and error propagation \KeyConcepts The derivative as a limit of a difference quotient and as an instantaneous rate of change / slope of the tangent line; differentiability implies continuity (but not conversely); the power, product, quotient, and chain rules; implicit differentiation; related rates; higher-order derivatives; linear approximation and differentials. \LearnObj Compute a derivative directly from its limit definition. Apply the power, product, quotient, and chain rules to differentiate combinations of functions. Perform implicit differentiation and solve related-rates problems. Differentiate trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, and inverse functions. Compute higher-order derivatives. Use linear approximation and differentials to estimate function values and propagate measurement error. \PreReq Limits and continuity (Chapter 3); the elementary function families of Chapter 1. \Hard Related-rates and implicit-differentiation word problems are consistently among the hardest topics in introductory calculus because they require translating a physical/biological scenario into an equation before any calculus is applied; combining the chain rule with implicit differentiation compounds this. Error propagation (Sec.\ 4.11) is a valuable but unfamiliar application for many students.

input_text: Course: Calculus I for Biological and Social Sciences. Section: 4. Cross-Cutting Themes and the Hardest Topics in the Course. Content: Discrete-to-continuous transitions. Students build strong discrete-time intuition in Chapter 2, then must re-learn stability and growth concepts in continuous form in Chapters 5 and 8. Explicitly cross-referencing the discrete and continuous versions of the same idea (e.g.\ discrete vs.\ continuous exponential growth, equilibrium stability of a recurrence equation vs.\ an ODE) shortens this transition. Rigor vs.\ intuition. The starred rigorous topics (\varepsilon--\delta limits, the Riemann integral construction, the Leibniz's Rule proof of the FTC) sit in tension with the course's model-building emphasis. Treating them as optional deep dives, clearly separated from the applied spine of the course, works better than interleaving them. Word-problem translation. Related rates, optimization, compartment/epidemic modeling, and Leslie-matrix demography all share the same underlying difficulty: converting a verbal description into equations before any calculus or algebra is applied. This is best taught as an explicit, repeated skill (define variables, state relationships, then compute) rather than assumed. Stacked symbolic technique. The chain rule combined with implicit differentiation, and partial fractions combined with substitution, both require executing several symbolic steps in the correct order; errors compound quickly, so scaffolded, partial-credit practice matters more here than in single-step computations. Eigenvalue-based qualitative reasoning. Eigenvalues recur as the organizing idea behind Leslie-matrix demography (Ch.\ 9), linear systems of ODEs (Ch.\ 11), and linearization of nonlinear systems (Ch.\ 10--11). Course: Calculus I for Biological and Social Sciences. Section: Course Description and Design Rationale. Content: Calculus for Biology and Medicine (4th ed.) is written for a one- or two-semester calculus sequence for life-science and social-science majors. Its twelve chapters run from precalculus review through probability and statistics, and the authors explicitly design sections marked with an asterisk (\opt) as optional ``instructor's choice'' material that can be trimmed without breaking the logical flow of the book. This document treats Chapters 1--6 as Calculus 1: precalculus review, discrete-time (recurrence) models, limits and continuity, differentiation, applications of differentiation, and integration through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. This mirrors how the book is used in two-semester bio-calculus tracks (e.g., the first course covers single-variable differential and integral calculus, and a second course, Calculus 2, covers Chapters 7--12: integration techniques, differential equations, linear algebra, multivariable calculus, systems of differential equations, and probability/statistics -- see Appendix~ app:calc2 ). Instructors on a one-semester-only track can compress the schedule in Section~ sec:schedule by cutting all asterisked (\opt) subsections. Distinguishing feature of this course: unlike a generic ``applied calculus'' course, every mathematical tool is introduced through a biological or social-science model first (population growth, drug absorption and elimination, enzyme kinetics, epidemics, allometric scaling, blood alcohol elimination, oxygen binding in blood) and only then treated with full mathematical rigor. Word-problem literacy -- turning a verbal description of a process into an equation -- is therefore treated as a first-class course objective, not an afterthought.
section_path: Course Description and Design Rationale

input_text: Course: Calculus I for Biological and Social Sciences. Section: Course-Level Student Learning Outcomes (SLOs). Content: By the end of the course, a successful student will be able to: Model discrete and continuous change. Translate a verbal description of a biological or social process into a recurrence equation, a limit statement, a derivative, or a definite integral, and interpret the mathematical result back in the original context. Evaluate limits and determine continuity of algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions, including limits at infinity and limits that require the sandwich theorem. Differentiate elementary, polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions using the formal definition and the rules of differentiation (sum, product, quotient, chain, implicit). Apply derivatives to find extrema, analyze monotonicity and concavity, solve optimization and related-rates problems, evaluate indeterminate forms (L'H\^opital's Rule), and produce derivative-informed graphs. Evaluate definite and indefinite integrals, state and apply both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and interpret a definite integral as cumulative change or an average value. Use technology (graphing calculators or spreadsheets) to visualize functions and data, iterate recurrence equations, and implement simple numerical methods (bisection, Newton--Raphson). Communicate quantitative reasoning, including the assumptions behind a mathematical model, its limitations, and how well it fits real or simulated data.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Front matter. Content: \maketitle This document presents a complete two-semester graduate course breakdown for Number Theory I, synthesized from the tables of contents of three classic textbooks: André Weil's Basic Number Theory \W, Jürgen Neukirch's Algebraic Number Theory \N, and Serge Lang's Algebraic Number Theory \Lg. The three books overlap substantially but differ in emphasis and level of abstraction: Neukirch is the most classical and pedagogically linear; Lang adds extensive analytic machinery (Tate's thesis, Tauberian theorems, Brauer--Siegel, explicit formulas); Weil gives the most abstract, adelic/idelic treatment and reaches class field theory via Brauer groups of simple algebras. The course below interleaves all three so that students see each major theorem from more than one point of view. \tableofcontents

Course: Number Theory I. Section: Course Description. Content: Number Theory I is a two-semester (year-long) graduate sequence covering the foundations of algebraic number theory, the theory of local fields, the adelic/idelic reformulation of classical algebraic number theory, the analytic theory of zeta and L-functions, and local and global class field theory. The course is designed for students who have completed a first-year graduate algebra sequence and wish to specialize in number theory, arithmetic geometry, or representation theory. The guiding philosophy is the function-field analogy: number fields behave like curves over finite fields, ideals like divisors, ramification like branching, and the Riemann--Roch theorem, zeta functions, and class field theory all express manifestations of a single underlying structure. Weil's adelic language is used throughout as the unifying framework, while Neukirch supplies the clearest linear exposition and Lang supplies the deepest analytic tools.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Prerequisites (Before Starting the Course). Content: Abstract algebra: groups, rings, modules, fields; Galois theory (fundamental theorem, normal/separable extensions, Galois groups of finite fields). Commutative algebra (light): localization, Noetherian rings, integral extensions, tensor products of rings and modules. (Reviewed from scratch in Unit 1.) Linear algebra: vector spaces, dual spaces, determinants, tensor and exterior products. Point-set topology: metric spaces, completeness, compactness; topological groups are helpful but not assumed. Complex analysis (needed starting Semester II, Unit 6): analytic continuation, contour integration, residues, Dirichlet series convergence. Harmonic analysis (helpful, reviewed as needed in Units 5 and 7): Fourier series/transforms on R, Haar measure on locally compact groups, Pontryagin duality. Representation theory of finite groups (helpful, reviewed in Unit 8): characters, induced representations.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Course-Level Learning Outcomes. Content: By the end of the two-semester sequence, students will be able to: Prove and apply the structure theory of Dedekind domains, ramification theory, and the Galois theory of number fields (decomposition/inertia groups, Frobenius elements). Work fluently with valuations, completions, and local fields, including Hensel's Lemma, ramification filtrations, and Weil's classification of locally compact fields. Construct the adele ring and idele group of a global field, prove the product formula, and use adelic finiteness (discreteness/cocompactness) to reprove classical finiteness theorems. Analyze zeta functions and L-series via Euler products and two independent proofs of the functional equation (Hecke's classical method and Tate's adelic method). Apply analytic number theory (Tauberian theorems, non-vanishing results, explicit formulas) to prime-counting and density questions, including the Chebotarev density theorem. Explain the cohomological/algebraic underpinnings of class field theory via simple algebras and Brauer groups. State, apply, and outline proofs of the main theorems of local and global class field theory, and translate fluently between the idelic and classical ideal-theoretic formulations. Recognize the function-field analogy (Riemann--Roch, zeta functions, class field theory) that unifies arithmetic and geometric perspectives.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Course Overview. Content: Math 617 is a first-semester graduate course in algebraic number theory. It assumes familiarity with graduate algebra and analysis at the qualifying-exam level and proceeds from the arithmetic of Dedekind domains through local and global fields to adèles and idèles, with Tate's thesis as an optional capstone topic if time permits. The course meets twice weekly (Tuesday/Thursday, 75 minutes) over a 15-week semester, with several sessions reserved for homework discussion. Grading is 100% homework, assigned weekly, with one or two randomly-selected problems graded for accuracy and the remainder for completion; the lowest homework score is dropped. This document expands the syllabus's four topic areas into a full breakdown: modules, chapters/reference correspondences, concepts, learning objectives, and difficult topics, together with the prerequisite background assumed at the outset.
section_path: Course Overview

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Overall Learning Objectives. Content: By the end of the course, students should be able to: Prove and apply the equivalent characterizations of Dedekind domains, and factor ideals uniquely in rings of integers. Compute ramification indices and residue degrees for primes in extensions of number fields, and use decomposition/inertia groups and the Frobenius element in the Galois case. Construct completions of a number field at a place and classify local fields, including applications of Hensel's Lemma. Use Minkowski's geometry of numbers to prove finiteness of the class number and Dirichlet's Unit Theorem. Construct the adèle ring and idèle group of a number field, work with their topology, and relate the idèle class group to classical arithmetic invariants. (If time permits) Explain Tate's reinterpretation of the functional equation of zeta and L-functions via harmonic analysis on adèles.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 1: Dedekind Domains and the Arithmetic of Number Rings. Content: Topics. Algebraic number fields and their rings of integers; Noetherian, integrally closed domains of Krull dimension~1; equivalent characterizations of a Dedekind domain; unique factorization of nonzero ideals into prime ideals; localization at a prime; fractional ideals; first look at the ideal class group. Key concepts. Integral closure \cdot Noetherian ring \cdot discrete valuation ring (DVR) \cdot fractional ideal \cdot unique factorization of ideals \cdot ideal class group. Reference chapters. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch.~I, \S1--3; Lang, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch.~I; Cassels--Fröhlich, Ch.~I. Learning objectives. State and prove the equivalence of the standard characterizations of a Dedekind domain (Noetherian + integrally closed + dimension~1 \iff every nonzero ideal factors uniquely into primes \iff localizations are DVRs). Factor concrete ideals in rings of integers of quadratic and cyclotomic fields. Distinguish factorization of ideals from (nonunique) factorization of elements. Difficult topics. Proving the equivalence of the various characterizations of Dedekind domains in full generality; the localization/globalization dictionary; recognizing when a given ring of integers fails to be a PID while remaining a Dedekind domain.
section_path: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 1: Dedekind Domains and the Arithmetic of Number Rings

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 2: Ramification Theory. Content: Topics. Decomposition of primes in an extension L/K; ramification index e and residue degree f; the fundamental identity \sum e_i f_i = [L:K]; behavior in Galois extensions; decomposition group and inertia group; the Frobenius element; the different and the discriminant; tame versus wild ramification; higher ramification groups. Key concepts. e, f, g \cdot decomposition group \cdot inertia group \cdot Frobenius automorphism \cdot different ideal \cdot discriminant \cdot tame/wild ramification. Reference chapters. Neukirch, Ch.~I, \S4--8, Ch.~III (Frobenius, discriminant); Lang, Ch.~I--III; Cassels--Fröhlich, Ch.~I--II. Learning objectives. Determine how a rational prime splits in a Galois number field via the Frobenius element (e.g.\ using factorization of the minimal polynomial mod p). Compute the discriminant of a number field and identify ramified primes from it. Explain the relationship between the decomposition group, inertia group, and the Galois group of the residue extension. Difficult topics. Wild ramification and the structure of higher ramification groups; the precise relationship between the different and the discriminant (conductor--discriminant considerations); ramification in non-Galois extensions.
section_path: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 2: Ramification Theory

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 3: Valuations, Completions, and Local Fields. Content: Topics. Archimedean and non-archimedean absolute values; Ostrowski's theorem classifying absolute values on \Q; completions of a field with respect to a valuation; construction of \Q_p; local fields and their classification; Hensel's Lemma and its applications; extensions of local fields; unramified versus totally ramified extensions; filtration of the unit group. Key concepts. Valuation \cdot completion \cdot p-adic numbers \cdot Hensel's Lemma \cdot local field \cdot unramified extension \cdot totally ramified extension \cdot unit filtration. Reference chapters. Neukirch, Ch.~II; Lang, Ch.~II; Weil, Basic Number Theory, Ch.~I--II. Learning objectives. Construct the completion of a number field at a given place and identify it explicitly for small examples. Apply Hensel's Lemma to determine solvability of polynomial equations in \Q_p or \Z_p. Classify the extensions of \Q_p of a given degree into unramified and (totally) ramified pieces. Difficult topics. The structure theorem for local fields in the wildly ramified case; the filtration of principal units and its Galois-module structure; correctly relating local ramification data back to the global picture from Module~2.
section_path: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 3: Valuations, Completions, and Local Fields

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 4: Global Fields and the Geometry of Numbers. Content: Topics. Places (archimedean and non-archimedean) of a number field; the product formula; Minkowski's geometry of numbers (lattices, convex bodies); finiteness of the ideal class number; Dirichlet's Unit Theorem; the regulator. Key concepts. Place \cdot product formula \cdot lattice \cdot Minkowski bound \cdot class number finiteness \cdot unit group rank \cdot regulator. Reference chapters. Neukirch, Ch.~I, \S5--7; Lang, Ch.~V; Cassels--Fröhlich, Ch.~II. Learning objectives. Prove finiteness of the class number using Minkowski's convex body theorem. State and use Dirichlet's Unit Theorem to determine the rank of the unit group of a ring of integers. Compute Minkowski bounds and use them to determine class numbers of small number fields. Difficult topics. The full proof of Dirichlet's Unit Theorem (logarithmic embedding into Euclidean space, lattice discreteness/cocompactness argument); correctly setting up Minkowski's theorem for a given signature (r_1, r_2).
section_path: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 4: Global Fields and the Geometry of Numbers

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 5: Adèles and Idèles. Content: Topics. Restricted direct products of topological groups; construction of the adèle ring A_K and the idèle group I_K; the topology on A_K and I_K; discreteness and cocompactness of K in A_K; the idèle class group C_K = I_K/K^\times; relating C_K to the ideal class group and the unit group; brief statement of Artin reciprocity as a bridge to class field theory. Key concepts. Restricted direct product \cdot adèle ring \cdot idèle group \cdot idèle class group \cdot strong approximation. Reference chapters. Neukirch, Ch.~VI, \S1--3; Weil, Basic Number Theory, Ch.~IV; Lang, Ch.~VII. Learning objectives. Construct the restricted direct product topology and verify A_K is a locally compact topological ring. Prove that K embeds discretely and cocompactly in A_K. Relate the structure of the idèle class group C_K to the class number and unit group computed in Module~4. Difficult topics. The restricted product topology (a genuinely new point-set topology construction for most students); the discreteness/cocompactness proof; the strong approximation theorem; keeping straight the several closely related but distinct objects ( A_K^\times, I_K, C_K).
section_path: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 5: Adèles and Idèles

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Detailed Module Breakdown > Module 6 (Optional): Tate's Thesis. Content: Topics. Additive and multiplicative characters of a local field; self-dual Haar measure and the local Fourier transform; local zeta functions and their functional equations; Schwartz--Bruhat functions on A_K; the global zeta integral; Poisson summation on the adèles; the analytic continuation and functional equation of the Riemann zeta function (and, more generally, Hecke L-functions) recovered via Tate's method. Key concepts. Additive/multiplicative character \cdot self-dual measure \cdot local zeta function \cdot Schwartz--Bruhat space \cdot adelic Poisson summation \cdot global functional equation. Reference chapters. J.\ Tate, Fourier Analysis in Number Fields and Hecke's Zeta-Functions (1950 thesis); Lang, Ch.~XIV; Cassels--Fröhlich, Ch.~XV (Tate's article). Learning objectives. State and outline a proof of the local functional equation for the local zeta function at a place of K. Derive the classical functional equation of \zeta(s) as a special case of the global Tate zeta integral. Explain, at a high level, how Tate's approach unifies the archimedean and non-archimedean cases via adelic harmonic analysis. Difficult topics. Choosing compatible self-dual additive characters/measures across all places simultaneously; convergence and analytic continuation of the global zeta integral; the role of Poisson summation in producing the functional equation. This module is the most analytically demanding in the course and depends on comfort with basic Fourier analysis on locally compact abelian groups.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification. Content: Weeks 1--4 (Sessions 1--8). Goal: establish the ring-theoretic foundations --- Dedekind domains, ideal factorization, and ramification in extensions --- that underlie everything else in the course.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Dedekind Domains: Definitions and Characterizations. Content: Core concepts Noetherian, integrally closed, Krull dimension one (every nonzero prime is maximal) Equivalent characterizations: localization at every prime is a DVR; every nonzero fractional ideal is invertible Examples: \OK for a number field K, coordinate rings of smooth affine curves, PIDs Non-example: non-maximal orders, e.g.\ \Z[\sqrt-3] Learning objectives Explain the equivalent characterizations of a Dedekind domain and prove their equivalence Derive that \OK is a Dedekind domain from integrality and finiteness properties Apply localization arguments to reduce global ring-theoretic questions to the DVR case Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show that a PID is a Dedekind domain. Rubric: PID \Rightarrow Noetherian (ACC on ideals); UFD \Rightarrow integrally closed; nonzero primes in a PID are generated by irreducibles, hence maximal. [Q2 (advanced).] Let A = \Z[\sqrt-3]. Exhibit an element of Frac(A) integral over A but not in A, and conclude A is not Dedekind. Answer: \tfrac1+\sqrt-32 satisfies x^2-x+1=0 and lies in O_\Q(\sqrt-3)=\Z[\tfrac1+\sqrt-32], but not in A.
section_path: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Dedekind Domains: Definitions and Characterizations

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Fractional Ideals, Unique Factorization, and the Ideal Class Group. Content: Core concepts Fractional ideals and their group structure under multiplication Unique factorization of ideals into primes (existence and uniqueness) The ideal class group Cl(K) = fractional ideals modulo principal ideals Finiteness of Cl(K) (stated here; proved in Module 2 via Minkowski theory) Learning objectives Prove unique factorization of ideals in a Dedekind domain Compute the ideal class group in small examples Explain the relationship between class number one and unique factorization of elements Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show every nonzero fractional ideal of a Dedekind domain is invertible. Rubric: prove local invertibility at each prime using the DVR structure, then glue. [Q2 (advanced).] Compute Cl(\Q(\sqrt-5)) by exhibiting a non-principal ideal. Rubric: factor (2,1+\sqrt-5) as a prime above 2, show non-principal via a norm argument, show its square is principal; conclude Cl(K)\cong \Z/2.
section_path: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Fractional Ideals, Unique Factorization, and the Ideal Class Group

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Extensions of Dedekind Domains: Decomposition of Primes. Content: Core concepts The integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite extension is again Dedekind Factorization p\OL = \prod P_i^e_i in an extension L/K The ideal norm and its multiplicativity Learning objectives Derive the factorization p\OL = \prod P_i^e_i from unique factorization Compute prime factorizations in specific number field extensions Apply the norm map to relate ideal factorization to field degree Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Factor (2) in \Z[i]. Answer: (2) = (1+i)^2, ramified since 2 \mid disc(\Q(i)). [Q2 (advanced).] Determine how 5 and 11 factor in \Q(\zeta_5). Rubric: 5 is totally ramified since 5\mid disc(\Q(\zeta_5)); the splitting of 11 is governed by the order of 11 mod 5.
section_path: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Extensions of Dedekind Domains: Decomposition of Primes

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Ramification Index, Residue Degree, and the Fundamental Identity. Content: Core concepts Definitions of ramification index e_i and residue degree f_i The fundamental identity \sum e_i f_i = [L:K]; constant e,f when L/K is Galois Split, inert, and ramified primes, with examples Learning objectives Derive \sum e_i f_i = n from the structure of \OL \otimes_\OK \OK/p Classify primes as split/inert/ramified in quadratic and cyclotomic fields Apply the identity to compute decomposition types from factorization data Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify \sum e_if_i = n for the factorization of (2) in \Z[i]. Answer: e=2, f=1, n=2: 2\cdot 1 = 2. \checkmark [Q2 (advanced).] Give a non-Galois cubic field where the primes above some p have differing e_i,f_i. Rubric: e.g.\ x^3-x-1; in a non-Galois extension e_i,f_i need not be constant across the primes above p, unlike the Galois case.
section_path: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Ramification Index, Residue Degree, and the Fundamental Identity

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 1: Dedekind Domains and Ramification > Discriminant, Different, and Dedekind's Ramification Theorem. Content: Core concepts The different ideal \mathfrakd_L/K and its relation to ramification The discriminant as the norm of the different Dedekind's theorem: p ramifies in L iff p \mid disc(L/K) Tame versus wild ramification Learning objectives Explain the relationship between the different, the discriminant, and ramification Derive Dedekind's ramification criterion from properties of the different Distinguish tame from wild ramification and identify which primes can be wildly ramified Historically hard. Why: notational overload (different vs.\ discriminant, ideal norm vs.\ field norm) compounds with a genuine abstraction jump into wild ramification, which has no analogue in the tame case. Mitigation: work tame ramification fully with explicit quadratic-field examples first; use a side-by-side table contrasting different vs.\ discriminant before stating Dedekind's theorem in general. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute disc(\Q(\sqrt d)) for squarefree d and identify the ramified primes. Answer: disc=d or 4d depending on d \bmod 4; ramified primes are exactly those dividing it. [Q2 (advanced).] Explain why wild ramification at p requires p \mid e, and construct an example. Rubric: tame ramification needs e coprime to the residue characteristic; \Q_p(p^1/p)/\Q_p via the Eisenstein polynomial x^p-p is totally, wildly ramified.

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Number Fields and Global Fields: Rings of Integers Revisited. Content: Core concepts Global fields: number fields and function fields over finite fields, as a unifying perspective Places of a global field: archimedean and non-archimedean \OK's ideal theory recast in the global-field/local-field language used going forward Learning objectives Explain the analogy between number fields and function fields as global fields Enumerate the places of a given number field (real, complex, finite) Situate \OK's ideal theory within the local/global framework Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] List the places of \Q(i). Answer: one complex place (r_1=0, r_2=1); non-archimedean places correspond to primes of \Z[i]. [Q2 (advanced).] Compare places of F_q(t) with places of \Q, and identify the ``infinite place'' of F_q(t). Rubric: places of F_q(t) correspond to monic irreducibles plus the degree valuation at infinity; note the disanalogy that F_q(t) has no true archimedean place.
section_path: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Number Fields and Global Fields: Rings of Integers Revisited

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Absolute Values and Completions; p-adic Numbers. Content: Core concepts Absolute values on a field; equivalence; Ostrowski's theorem for \Q Completion with respect to an absolute value; construction of \Qp \Zp as an inverse limit; p-adic expansions Learning objectives Prove Ostrowski's theorem classifying absolute values on \Q Construct \Qp both via completion and via inverse limits, and show these agree Apply p-adic expansions to solve concrete equations Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify |\cdot|_p satisfies the ultrametric inequality. Rubric: follows from additivity properties of the p-adic valuation v_p. [Q2 (advanced).] Does \sqrt 2 exist in \Q_7? If so, find its first three p-adic digits. Answer: 3^2 \equiv 2 \bmod 7, so by Hensel's lemma \sqrt 2 \in \Q_7; digits obtained by Hensel lifting.
section_path: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Absolute Values and Completions; p-adic Numbers

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Structure of Local Field Extensions; Hensel's Lemma. Content: Core concepts Hensel's Lemma and consequences (lifting roots, structure of \Zp^*) Uniqueness of the extension of an absolute value to a finite extension Unramified extensions \leftrightarrow residue field extensions; totally ramified extensions \leftrightarrow Eisenstein polynomials Structure theorem: every finite extension decomposes as unramified-then-totally-ramified Learning objectives Apply Hensel's Lemma to lift factorizations and determine unit structure Classify finite extensions of \Qp into unramified and totally ramified pieces Construct explicit local extensions via Eisenstein polynomials Historically hard. Why: the ``lifting'' intuition (a p-adic Newton's method) is unfamiliar, and holding the unramified/totally-ramified dichotomy in mind as two distinct extension mechanisms is easy to conflate. Mitigation: present Hensel's Lemma explicitly as p-adic Newton's method with a numerical example first, then build the dichotomy from two contrasting explicit extensions. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Use Hensel's Lemma to show \Zp^* contains all (p-1)-th roots of unity, p odd. Rubric: apply Hensel to x^p-1-1 using simple roots mod p from Fermat's little theorem. [Q2 (advanced).] Construct the unramified extension of \Qp of degree n, and contrast with \Qp(p^1/n). Rubric: unramified: adjoin roots of unity generating the degree-n residue field extension; ramified: Eisenstein
section_path: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Structure of Local Field Extensions; Hensel's Lemma

Content: unramified extension of \Qp of degree n, and contrast with \Qp(p^1/n). input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Local-Global Compatibility: Places, Completions, and the Product Formula. Content: Core concepts Normalized absolute values at each place; the product formula \prod_v |x|_v = 1 Relating global ideal factorization to local completions K_v Weak approximation Learning objectives Prove the product formula for number fields Explain how localizing \OK at a prime recovers the local field K_v Apply weak approximation to construct elements with prescribed local behavior Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify \prod_v |2|_v = 1 for K = \Q. Answer: |2|_2 = 1/2, |2|_\infty = 2, all other |2|_v = 1; product =1. [Q2 (advanced).] Use the product formula to constrain elements of \OK that are small at every archimedean place and integral at every finite place. Rubric: the product formula forces a global product-of-one constraint; relate to Kronecker's theorem characterizing roots of unity.
section_path: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Local-Global Compatibility: Places, Completions, and the Product Formula

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Minkowski Theory: Geometry of Numbers, Finiteness of the Class Number. Content: Core concepts The Minkowski embedding K \hookrightarrow R^r_1\times C^r_2 and the lattice \OK Minkowski's convex body theorem The Minkowski bound; finiteness of Cl(K), completing Module 1 Learning objectives Derive the Minkowski bound and use it to compute class numbers in examples Prove finiteness of the ideal class group via the geometry of numbers Apply the Minkowski embedding to bound discriminants Historically hard. Why: this is a genuine change of category, from ideal-theoretic to geometric/volume-based reasoning, and the convex body theorem's soft counting argument is unlike the explicit proofs used so far. Mitigation: draw the 2-dimensional lattice picture for a real quadratic field before the general proof; give a step-by-step worked template for the Minkowski bound. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute the Minkowski bound for \Q(\sqrt-5) and determine the class number. Answer: bound \approx 2.85, so only p=2 needs checking, giving class number 2. [Q2 (advanced).] Prove Minkowski's convex body theorem. Rubric: pigeonhole argument on translates of half the body; volume exceeding the covolume forces overlap.
section_path: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Minkowski Theory: Geometry of Numbers, Finiteness of the Class Number

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Dirichlet's Unit Theorem. Content: Core concepts The unit group \OK^*: torsion (roots of unity) and free part Statement: rank r_1 + r_2 - 1 The logarithmic embedding and the geometry-of-numbers proof strategy Learning objectives State and explain the structure of \OK^* via Dirichlet's unit theorem Derive the rank formula r_1+r_2-1 using the logarithmic embedding Compute fundamental units in small examples Historically hard. Why: the logarithmic embedding reuses the Minkowski-theory machinery in a new embedding, and bookkeeping the rank r_1+r_2-1 against the torsion kernel is a common source of off-by-one errors. Mitigation: work the rank computation for a real and an imaginary quadratic field side by side before the general proof. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute the unit rank of \Q(\sqrt2) and \Q(\sqrt-2), and find a fundamental unit for \Q(\sqrt2). Answer: ranks 1 and 0 respectively; fundamental unit 1+\sqrt2. [Q2 (advanced).] Derive r_1+r_2-1 from the logarithmic embedding \OK^*\to R^r_1+r_2. Rubric: image lies in a hyperplane by the product formula; discreteness plus boundedness gives a full-rank lattice in that hyperplane.
section_path: Module 2: Global and Local Fields > Dirichlet's Unit Theorem

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles. Content: Weeks 10--12 (Sessions 19--24). Goal: assemble all completions of a global field into the adèle ring and idèle group, developing the topological and measure-theoretic structure needed for Tate's thesis.
section_path: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Restricted Direct Products and the Adèle Ring. Content: Core concepts The restricted direct product construction \prod'(K_v, O_v) The adèle ring \A_K as a restricted product over all places K embeds diagonally in \A_K; K is discrete (cocompactness stated, proved in \S3.2) Learning objectives Construct \A_K as a restricted direct product and verify it is a topological ring Explain why restricting to ``almost all O_v'' is necessary for local compactness Identify K as a discrete subring of \A_K Historically hard. Why: the restricted-product topology (``almost all coordinates in O_v'') is unlike any topology seen before this course. Mitigation: build up from finite sub-products (``S-adèles'') as a directed limit before taking the full restricted product. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show \prod'(\Q_p,\Zp) together with R is locally compact. Rubric: basic opens are products of opens at finitely many places times \prod \Zp elsewhere; local compactness follows from compactness of \Zp. [Q2 (advanced).] Show \Q embeds as a discrete subring of \A_\Q. Rubric: find a neighborhood of 0 meeting \Q only at 0, using that a rational number bounded archimedean and integral everywhere finite must be an integer.
section_path: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Restricted Direct Products and the Adèle Ring

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Topology, Local Compactness, and Self-Duality of Adèles. Content: Core concepts Local compactness of \A_K Pontryagin duality background (via the measure-theory prerequisite) Self-duality \A_K \cong \widehat\A_K via a nontrivial additive character Learning objectives Prove local compactness of \A_K from the restricted-product topology Explain the construction of self-duality via an additive character Apply Pontryagin duality formalism in the adelic setting Historically hard. Why: self-duality via a character is often presented too quickly, obscuring why the choice of character matters. Mitigation: construct the standard character on \A_\Q/\Q explicitly, local component by local component, before asserting self-duality in general. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show \A_K/K is compact, given an explicit fundamental domain. Rubric: exhibit a compact fundamental domain as a product of bounded local pieces. [Q2 (advanced).] Construct \psi = \prod \psi_v on \A_\Q/\Q explicitly and verify it is nontrivial on \A_\Q but trivial on \Q. Rubric: \psi_\infty(x)=e^-2\pi i x, \psi_p(x)=e^2\pi i \x\_p; sum of fractional parts over all places is an integer.
section_path: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Topology, Local Compactness, and Self-Duality of Adèles

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > The Idèle Group and Idèle Class Group. Content: Core concepts Idèles \A_K^* as units of \A_K, with their own finer restricted-product topology The idèle class group C_K = \A_K^*/K^* Relation between C_K and the classical ideal class group Cl(K) Learning objectives Explain why the idèle topology is strictly finer than the subspace topology from \A_K Derive the surjection from idèles to fractional ideals and identify its kernel Relate the idèle class group to the classical ideal class group Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show (x_v) \mapsto \prod P_v^v(x_v) is a surjective homomorphism from idèles to fractional ideals, and identify the kernel. Answer: kernel is the group of ``unit idèles.'' [Q2 (advanced).] Show C_K surjects onto Cl(K), and identify the kernel. Rubric: compose Q1's surjection with the quotient by principal ideals; kernel involves global units and archimedean components.
section_path: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > The Idèle Group and Idèle Class Group

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Compactness of the Norm-One Idèle Class Group. Content: Core concepts The norm map |\cdot|: \A_K^* \to R_>0; norm-one idèles \A_K^1 Theorem: C_K^1 = \A_K^1/K^* is compact This single theorem encodes both finiteness of the class number and Dirichlet's unit theorem Learning objectives Prove compactness of C_K^1, building on Minkowski theory Explain how this theorem unifies finiteness of Cl(K) and the unit theorem Apply compactness to derive structural facts about C_K Historically hard. Why: this is the conceptual climax of the local-global story, and its proof repackages Minkowski theory and Dirichlet's unit theorem in idelic language --- students who haven't internalized those two results will find this proof opaque. Mitigation: give an explicit dictionary mapping each step of the classical arguments to its idelic reformulation before the proof. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Explain why compactness of C_K^1 implies finiteness of the class number. Rubric: continuous image of compact is compact; the ideal-valued map has finitely many fiber classes. [Q2 (advanced).] Explain how compactness of C_K^1 also encodes Dirichlet's unit theorem. Rubric: relate the kernel of the archimedean norm map on units to the logarithmic embedding lattice from \S2.6.
section_path: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Compactness of the Norm-One Idèle Class Group

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Haar Measure, Fundamental Domains, and Volume Computations. Content: Core concepts Existence/uniqueness of Haar measure on \A_K and \A_K^* An explicit fundamental domain for K in \A_K; volume in terms of the discriminant Measure normalization conventions used later in Tate's thesis Learning objectives Construct Haar measure on \A_K from local Haar measures at each place Compute vol(K\backslash\A_K) in terms of the discriminant d_K Apply measure normalization conventions needed for zeta integrals Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] With vol(\Zp)=1 at each finite place, compute vol(\A_\Q/\Q). Answer: volume =1, matching d_\Q=1 up to normalization. [Q2 (advanced).] Express vol(\A_K/K) in terms of d_K for general K, and explain its role in Tate's thesis. Rubric: vol = |d_K|^1/2 up to convention; enters as a normalization factor in the residue of the global zeta integral at s=1.
section_path: Module 3: Adèles and Idèles > Haar Measure, Fundamental Domains, and Volume Computations

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits). Content: Weeks 13--15 (Sessions 25--30, contingent on pace). Goal: use the adelic/idelic machinery to give a uniform, harmonic-analytic proof of analytic continuation and the functional equation for the Dedekind zeta function and Hecke L-functions, following Tate's local-to-global method.
section_path: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits)

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits) > Schwartz--Bruhat Functions and Local Zeta Integrals. Content: Core concepts Schwartz--Bruhat spaces at archimedean and non-archimedean places Local zeta integrals Z(f,\chi,s) = \int f(x)\,\chi(x)\,|x|^s\, d^*x Local convergence, meromorphic continuation, and local L-factors Learning objectives Define Schwartz--Bruhat functions at each type of place with explicit examples Compute local zeta integrals for standard test functions Derive local L-factors from explicit computations at unramified places Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute Z(f,\chi,s) for f = 1_ O_p, \chi unramified, non-archimedean. Answer: a geometric series yielding (1-\chi(\pi)q^-s)^-1, the expected local L-factor. [Q2 (advanced).] Compute the archimedean zeta integral for f(x)=e^-\pi x^2 with \chi trivial. Rubric: Gaussian integral yielding a factor of \Gamma(s/2) up to normalization.
section_path: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits) > Schwartz--Bruhat Functions and Local Zeta Integrals

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits) > Local Functional Equation and Local L-Factors. Content: Core concepts Local Fourier transform and self-dual Haar measure The local functional equation relating Z(f,\chi,s) and Z(\hat f,\chi^-1,1-s) Local epsilon factors Learning objectives State and explain the local functional equation for zeta integrals Derive the local functional equation at unramified places via explicit Fourier transforms Apply the local functional equation to compute epsilon factors in simple cases Historically hard. Why: the Fourier-analytic manipulation is analytically unfamiliar for students whose recent training has been algebraic, and epsilon factors are often introduced as an unmotivated ``fudge factor.'' Mitigation: compute the functional equation fully and explicitly for K=\Q_p, unramified, before the general statement, showing exactly where the epsilon factor arises. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify the local functional equation at an unramified place directly from the \S4.1 computation. Rubric: compare the two local L-factors; epsilon factor equals 1 in the unramified case. [Q2 (advanced).] Compute the local epsilon factor for a ramified quadratic character of \Q_p^*. Rubric: a normalized Gauss-sum computation.
section_path: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits) > Local Functional Equation and Local L-Factors

input_text: Course: Number Theory I. Section: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits) > Global Zeta Integrals, Poisson Summation, and the Global Functional Equation. Content: Core concepts The global zeta integral over idèle classes, factoring as a product of local integrals Poisson summation on \A_K, using self-duality (\S3.2) and the fundamental domain (\S3.5) Analytic continuation and functional equation; recovering \zeta_K(s) and Hecke L-functions Learning objectives Derive analytic continuation of the global zeta integral using Poisson summation Explain how the global functional equation follows from local functional equations plus Poisson summation Apply Tate's method to recover the classical functional equation of \zeta_K(s) Historically hard. Why: this step synthesizes nearly the entire course into one argument, and adelic Poisson summation is a non-obvious generalization of the classical formula on R. Mitigation: review classical Poisson summation on R as a warm-up, then present the adelic version as the same formula with K replacing \Z and \A_K replacing R. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] State classical Poisson summation on R and give its adelic dictionary. Rubric: match each classical term (sum over \Z, Fourier transform on R) to its adelic analogue. [Q2 (advanced).] Sketch how Tate's method recovers the functional equation of \zeta(s) for K=\Q. Rubric: split the zeta integral at |x|=1, apply adelic Poisson summation to relate the two pieces, obtain continuation and \xi(s)=\xi(1-s).
section_path: Module 4: Tate's Thesis (If Time Permits) > Global Zeta Integrals, Poisson Summation, and the Global Functional Equation
